facts.text: Shenandoah Retreat’s historic core centers on the 1799 Retreat house built by Revolutionary War veteran Thomas Parker on 1,120 acres he acquired from the Wormley family in 1794.
The area was part of the 5‑million‑acre Northern Neck Proprietary granted to Thomas Fairfax in 1649, sparking mid‑18th‑century settlement by English planters and German immigrants.
During the Civil War’s Valley Campaign, Union forces crossed the Shenandoah River at Parker’s Ford—adjacent to the Retreat property—while fighting Confederate troops led by Jubal A. A. Smith.
Today, Shenandoah Retreat balances preserved Civil War heritage with suburban residential life, drawing residents who enjoy the valley’s natural scenery and proximity to Washington, D.C.
Soils here derive from limestone and dolomite, producing fertile loamy textures that historically supported crop production and pastures after liming and fertilization.
The region enjoys a humid subtropical climate, averaging 38 inches of rain annually, with January lows near 27 °F and July highs around 87 °F.
